Article Title: Gaps in Meta policy to protect copyright material, says judge
Article Text:
A content creator moved HC alleging that genuine creators such as him were denied access to the copyright tool

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Delhi high court Wednesday asked Meta to explain the criteria it follows to grant users access to its copyright management tool, Rights Manager, for Facebook and Instagram.A content creator moved HC alleging that genuine creators such as him were denied access to the copyright tool and, thus, were unable to protect their original content whose ownership was claimed by scammers using Rights Manager.Justice Anup J Bhambhani criticised the platform’s restrictive policy. “Why does everybody not have access to it then? It is like giving the key to the robber and not to the owner of the house,” it said.The judge said there appeared to be “some chinks in the armour, some loopholes” in the Meta policy on safeguarding the copyright material.Rights Manager enables pre-approved users to identify content uploaded on Facebook and Instagram and stake ownership as it permits them to monitor, block or act against such content.“Rights Manager is a video, audio and image-matching tool that we developed for rights holders of all sizes — from individual creators to media publishers, sports leagues, music labels and others — to identify and manage their content on Facebook and Instagram, including live videos,” the platform told the court.Meta submitted before HC that the copyright strikes against the plaintiff stood reversed and whatever content was removed has also been restored.It said the plaintiff’s accounts had never been suspended and remained accessible.HC then issued summons in the suit and posted the matter for hearing on Sept 24 along with a connected petition filed by another content creator.The second plea has alleged that the creator’s Instagram account was suspended following a copyright strike that was subsequently found to be false. The connected proceedings will also examine issues concerning the authority of social media platforms to suspend user profiles based on copyright infringement claims.
Article Summary: Delhi high court Wednesday asked Meta to explain the criteria it follows to grant users access to its copyright management tool, Rights Manager, for Facebook and Instagram. A content creator moved HC alleging that genuine creators such as him were denied access to the copyright tool. Justice Anup J Bhambhani criticised the platform’s restrictive policy.

Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is here as the company’s latest foldable smartphone under the pixel 11 series. The handset comes with an 8-inch inner display, and a 6.5-inch outer screen. It is powered by Google’s new Tensor G6 processor and 16GB RAM. The phone supports up to 512GB storage, a triple rear camera system, a 4,750mAh battery and Google's new HiLight feature. Other features on the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold include Android-based AI features powered by Gemini, IP68-rated water and dust resistance, and support for Qi2.2 wireless charging. Here’s a look at all features, pricing and availability of Pixel 11 Pro FoldGoogle Pixel 11 Pro Fold is offered in single RAM and storage variant. It packs 16GB RAM and 512GB storage and is priced at Rs 1,86,999. The handset comes in Olive colour variant.Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold will go on pre-order from today, August 12, with devices going on sale fromGoogle Pixel 11 Pro Fold comes with a 6.5-inch outer OLED display with a resolution of 1080 x 2342 pixels and an 8-inch inner OLED foldable display with a resolution of 2076 x 2152 pixels. Both displays support an adaptive refresh rate of 1Hz to 120Hz and peak brightness of up to 3,600 nits.The device measures 10.1mm when folded and 5.0mm when unfolded, and weighs 239 grams. It includes Google's new HiLight feature, which lets users receive alerts without looking at the screen.The smartphone is powered by the Google Tensor G6 processor with a Titan M3 security chip, 16GB RAM, and 512GB storage. The device also includes Car Crash Detection, Safety Check, Emergency Contacts, Android Earthquake Alerts, theft protection, stereo speakers, and Spatial Audio support.

Other features include Android-based AI features powered by Gemini, IP68-rated water and dust resistance, and support for Qi2.2 wireless charging.

Google Pixel 11 series has been launched. The company has officially taken the wraps off its next-generation Pixel lineup at its “Made by Google” hardware event, bringing three new phones: the Google Pixel 11, Google Pixel 11 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, with a new in-house chip, a powerful security setup and a fresh round of AI features built around Gemini. The company has also launched the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Google Pixel Watch 5 (in two sizes), a new colour of the Google Pixel Bunds Pro 2 and a bunch of accessories, including PixelSnap Ring Stand and PixelSnap charger with stand. Here's a complete breakdown of what is new and what it will cost you in India.The Google Pixel 11 starts at Rs 89,999 for the base 256GB model that comes with 12GB RAM. The Pixel 11 Pro price in India starts at Rs 1,19,999 for the base 256GB and the Pixel 11 Pro XL price in India starts at Rs 1,34,999. This means that the Pixel 11 series gets a Rs 10,000 price hike across models.Pre-orders for the series are now open through Google's own store as well as partner retailers with devices going on sale fromColour options also differ across the lineup: the Google Pixel Pro and Google Pixel Pro XL come in Canyon, Olive, Fog and a matte Obsidian finish, while the standard Google Pixel 11 gets its own palette of Frost, Pistachio, Hibiscus and Obsidian.All three phones stick with Google’s familiar Pixel design language, but the Pro models get a notably brighter, sharper screen. The Pixel 11 Pro comes with a 6.3-inch Super Actua display, while the Pro XL steps up to a larger 6.8-inch panel with both offering adaptive refresh rate that scales between 1Hz and 120Hz. The standard Pixel 11 gets a slightly smaller Actua display with a 60-120Hz range instead.Peak brightness on the Pro models can hit up to 3,600 nits, while the standard Pixel 11 tops out at 3,000 nits. All three models use Corning's Gorilla Glass Victus 2 for protection, with the Pro models adding an anti-scratch shield on top. One of the most highlighting changes in the phones is HiLight – an array of ambient LED lights built around the camera’s flash to give you light-based communications on the back of the phone.When your phone is face down, HiLight gently glows to give you a visual cue to pick up your phone, or stay in the moment.When it comes to performance and security, powering the entire lineup is Google’s new Tensor G6 chip, paired with a Titan M3 security coprocessor across all three models. Google is pitching this as a meaningful jump in on-device security, with a multi-layered setup that includes quantum-safe secure boot built directly into the hardware.Google Pixel phones have led the cameras department when it comes to point-and-shoot photography. The Google Pixel 11 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL share an identical camera setup: a 50MP wide lens, a 48MP ultrawide camera with macro focus, and a 48MP telephoto lens offering 5x optical zoom and up to 120x Pro Zoom. The standard Pixel 11 gets a slightly toned-down system: a 48MP wide camera, a 13MP ultrawide lens, and a 10.8MP telephoto sensor capped at 30x Super Zoom.On the front, the Pro models get a 42MP selfie camera, compared to 10.5MP on the standard Pixel 11. All three models support Google's usual suite of computational photography tools, including Night Sight, Astrophotography, Magic Eraser, Best Take, and the newer Edit with Ask Photos feature, which lets you make edits using natural-language prompts.Talking about battery, charging and durability, all three phones promise over 30 hours of battery life, backed by battery capacities ranging from 4,850mAh on the Pixel 11 Pro to up to 5,115mAh on the larger Google Pixel 11 Pro XL. All three also support Pixelsnap wireless charging at up to 25W, and come with an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance.Coming to the AI features and software, every model in the lineup ships with Gemini Intelligence built in, powered by Google's on-device Gemini Nano model. That includes access to Gemini Live for real-time conversational AI, along with Magic Cue, a feature designed to proactively surface relevant information based on what's happening on your screen. Google is also backing the lineup with a lengthy software commitment with all three phones are promised seven years of OS updates, security patches and Pixel Drop feature updates, running on Android 17 out of the box.
Article Summary: Google Pixel 11, Google Pixel 11 Pro and Google Pixel Pro XL have been launched in India. Pre-orders for the Pixel 11 series are open through Google's own as well as partner retailers with devices going on sale from August 20. The company has officially taken the wraps off its next-generation Pixel lineup at its “Made by Google’s” hardware event.

Article Title: TSMC and Taiwan researchers engineered an interface only 0.42 nanometers thick to improve next-generation MoS2 transistors
Article Text:
Representational AI photo

Focus on Atomic Boundary

Why interface matters

Science Daily photo

0.42-nanometre buffer layer

Relevance for future chips

Researchers from Taiwan's National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) and TSMC Corporate Research have developed a new way to improve transistors made from atomically thin materials. They focuses on the tiny boundary where two materials meet, which allowed them to build transistors with an extremely thin insulating layer while maintaining strong electrical performance.According to Science Daily, atomically thin semiconductors have been studied for more than a decade because some can be just one atom thick while still showing useful electrical properties. Such materials could allow transistors to become smaller, faster and more energy efficient than conventional silicon-based devices.However, making these very thin transistors work well has been difficult. One major problem involves the gate dielectric, an extremely thin insulating layer that helps control the movement of electrons. Making it thinner can improve transistor control, but when it is placed on an atomically thin semiconductor, problems can develop at the boundary between the two materials. These can interfere with electron movement and reduce performance.The new study, published in Nature Electronics, addresses this problem by engineering the atomic interface between the semiconductor and the insulating layer.The NYCU team worked with TSMC Corporate Research to engineer the narrow region where the two materials meet. Instead of focusing only on finding a new semiconductor, the researchers changed the interface itself.The team used monolayer molybdenum disulfide, or MoS2, as the semiconductor. A monolayer is a material that is only one layer of atoms thick. The researchers first placed an ultrathin epitaxial aluminium layer directly on the MoS2.They then oxidised the aluminium to create an aluminium oxide layer about 0.42 nanometres thick. After this, they added a high-κ hafnium oxide gate dielectric, an insulating material that can provide strong electrical control while remaining very thin.The 0.42-nanometre aluminium oxide layer acted as a buffer between the MoS2 and hafnium oxide. It created a smoother surface, helping the hafnium oxide grow more uniformly, while also reducing unwanted electrical interactions between the two materials."For many years, efforts to improve atomically thin transistors have largely focused on discovering better semiconductor materials," said Professor Wen-Hao Chang, the study's corresponding author from NYCU. "Our research shows that the atomic interface between materials can be just as important. By engineering that boundary, we were able to reduce one of the fundamental trade-offs that has limited two-dimensional transistors for many years," he added.Atomically thin semiconductors create a particular challenge because their surfaces do not have dangling bonds. This makes it difficult to grow an extremely thin dielectric layer evenly across the surface.Standard deposition methods can leave gaps and defects at the interface. These can create electrical disorder and reduce carrier mobility, which refers to how easily electrons move through a material.Researchers have explored different dielectric materials, molecular seed layers and other oxide deposition methods. However, achieving a very thin equivalent oxide thickness, strong electrostatic control and high carrier mobility at the same time remains difficult.The challenge is especially important for wafer-scale CVD-grown monolayer MoS2. CVD, or chemical vapour deposition, is a method used to produce thin material layers over a larger area.The researchers' approach was to redesign the interface rather than replace the semiconductor or gate dielectric. They placed the ultrathin epitaxial aluminium layer on monolayer MoS2 and oxidised it to produce the 0.42-nanometre aluminium oxide layer. The high-κ hafnium oxide was then added on top.The team built short-channel top-gate transistors using CVD-grown monolayer MoS2. The devices had an equivalent oxide thickness of about one nanometre.Tests showed low leakage current and minimal hysteresis. Hysteresis refers to unwanted differences in a transistor's electrical response depending on its previous operating condition.The transistors reached a maximum transconductance of 0.45 mS μm-1, with channel lengths of about 100 nanometres. Transconductance measures how strongly a transistor's current responds when the gate voltage changes.The devices combined a very thin dielectric with strong electrical control and continued carrier transport, a combination that has been difficult to achieve in atomically thin transistors.The findings highlight the growing importance of interfaces as transistor components become smaller. When materials are only a few atomic layers thick, the region where two materials meet can strongly affect how the device performs."When transistor components become only a few atomic layers thick, the interface is no longer simply the boundary between materials, it becomes an active part of the device," said Professor Tsung-En Lee, the study's corresponding author. "Learning to engineer these interfaces with atomic precision opens new opportunities for designing future semiconductor devices that would be difficult to achieve by changing individual materials alone," professor Lee added.The researchers believe the approach could contribute to future two-dimensional electronics. Using CVD-grown monolayer MoS2 also brings the work closer to materials and processes that could eventually be considered for wafer-scale manufacturing.
Article Summary: Researchers from Taiwan's National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University have developed a new way to improve transistors made from atomically thin materials. They focuses on the tiny boundary where two materials meet, which allowed them to build transistors with an extremely thin insulating layer.

Article Title: FDA clears hearing aid feature on Samsung Galaxy Buds
Article Text:
Samsung introduced the Personal Sound Amplification Product (PSAP) feature on Galaxy Buds+ in 2020

Samsung announced that its Galaxy Buds Hearing Aid feature has received US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance, enabling compatible Galaxy Buds to serve as an over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aid, offering users 18 years and older a convenient solution for addressing perceived mild to moderate hearing loss. Users can also diagnose their hearing with the Galaxy Buds Hearing Test feature, which is registered as a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and provides medical-grade results.Commenting on the launch, Hon Pak, Senior Vice President and Head of the Digital Health Team for the Mobile eXperience (MX) Business at Samsung Electronics said “Hearing health is a vital component of our overall well-being, profoundly impacting how we communicate, connect with loved ones and engage with the world,” adding “With the latest clearance from the FDA, we are expanding access to hearing support and making proactive care effortless by integrating the Hearing Test and Hearing Aid functionality directly into the Galaxy Buds. ”Samsung introduced a Personal Sound Amplification Product (PSAP) feature on Galaxy Buds+ in 2020. The PSAP feature was clinically validated in 2021 as effective support for daily communication for those with hearing loss.To develop this new OTC solution, Samsung collaborated closely with the National Acoustic Laboratories (NAL) and Samsung Medical Center (SMC). The resulting technology is backed by robust clinical validation studies conducted at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, San Jose State University and the University of Memphis.Based on those results, the Hearing Aid feature amplifies the sounds users have difficulty hearing — such as high frequencies, surrounding whispers and distant voices — personalized to each user’s hearing profile.Samsung said the hearing aid also supports additional advanced features typically found in premium hearing aids, such as noise elimination and beamforming, which help focus sounds in front of the user and suppress background noise. The Hearing Aid and Hearing Test features will be available on Galaxy Buds 3 Pro and Galaxy Buds 4 Pro in the US and select approved markets in Q4 2026.
Article Summary: Samsung announced that its Galaxy Buds Hearing Aid feature has received US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance. The feature will be available on Galaxy Bud's 3 Pro and 4 Pro in the US and select approved markets in Q4 2026. Samsung introduced a Personal Sound Amplification Product (PSAP) feature on Galaxy buds+ in 2020.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Viral reels to drive TB awareness in Maharashtra
Article Text:
Poster for competition of reels

Pune:





From painted village walls to viral reels, India’s public health messaging is undergoing a makeover.A 24-year-old nursing student of a Sangli college got absorbed in creating an out-of-the-box reel to create awareness about tuberculosis, as the state on Wednesday announced Maharashtra ’s "Tuberculosis-Free India" reel competition for nurses and nursing students. The state public health department and Trained Nurses’ Association of India, Maharashtra branch, are its organisers.Dr Nilima Sonawane, deputy director of health services (nursing), said, “The younger nurses are tech savvy. They know how to shoot and edit videos. We see a lot of misinformation being propagated in the social media. So, we thought why not use the content made by our nurses, who will give accurate information. They are closest to the public and understand public queries.”She said, “We want to use their skills and information for the betterment of society. The initiative places nurses, not influencers, at the centre of digital communication, drawing on their experience to address TB symptoms, testing, treatment, nutrition, adherence and stigma. It will also ensure that the accurate information reaches the masses without creating fear or an unnecessary hype.”Dr Sonawane said, “Our nurses will use the local dialect, folklore or real-life stories. These will turn instruction into dialogue and help public retain the information longer than usual. Our nursing students have been making reels for various competitions. We observed that these were good content. With submissions closing on August 14, the campaign may signal a new language for public health communication and encourage healthcare workers to step up their game. ”She said, “Nurses from over 100 nursing colleges have been told to participate in the reels competition. The best reels would be used for the govt IEC (information, education and communication) campaigns. The nurses would be awarded for the same.”Tuberculosis is not merely a matter of medical treatment. It is associated with social misconceptions, fear and stigma. Therefore, alongside providing accurate information about the disease, it is essential to raise public awareness regarding symptom recognition, timely testing, treatment adherence (without interruption), proper nutrition and the avoidance of discrimination against patients. This competition offers a creative opportunity to convey these points to the public through reels.Dr Bhagwan Pawar, deputy director, in charge of public health department IEC, said, “This approach transforms health messages from mere 'preaching' into a dialogue connected to people’s daily lives. The initiative creates a unique synergy by combining the experience of nurses working in the field, the digital creativity of the youth and the vast reach of social media.”Pawar said, “This is a significant step towards a tuberculosis-free Maharashtra and India. It should not be viewed merely as a 'reel competition’, but rather as the beginning of a new language for public health awareness. After the creativity of nursing students merges with the power of social media, these reels can truly carry the message of tuberculosis eradication to every household.”
Article Summary: Nurses from over 100 colleges have been told to participate in the reels competition. The best reels would be used for the govt IEC (information, education and communication) campaigns. With submissions closing on August 14, the campaign may signal a new language for public health communication and encourage healthcare workers to step up their game.

Article Title: Two-storey house under construction collapses, destroys home nearby
Article Text:
AI image

Palakkad

:





A two-storey house that was under construction collapsed onto a neighbouring tiled-roof house at Vallikode in Palakkad on Tuesday afternoon. Both the buildings were destroyed in the incident. A man inside the tiled-roof house had a narrow escape as he ran out moments before the structure collapsed.The accident occurred around 2pm while construction was in progress. Locals alleged that the house was being built without maintaining the mandatory setback distance from the neighbouring property, raising concerns over possible violations of building rules.The tiled-roof house belonged to a daily-wage labourer. The five-member family has now lost their home, belongings and important documents in the incident.The owner of the two-storey house has reportedly offered to build a new house for the affected family. However, the family has been left without shelter until then.Panchayat officials and the police visited the site and launched an inquiry to determine the cause of the collapse and examine whether building regulations were violated.
Article Summary: A two-storey house that was under construction collapsed onto a neighbouring tiled-roof house at Vallikode in Palakkad. Locals alleged that the house was being built without maintaining the mandatory setback distance from the neighbouring property. Article Title: Archeologists discovered 7,000-year-old Neolithic burial grounds in France using electrical surveys
Article Text:
Coëby contains numerous megalithic monuments. Image Credit: Wikimedia commons

How did archeologists look beneath the 7,000-year-old mounds

Could those Neolithic mounds have been burial monuments

Image Credit: AI generated

What are Passy-type monuments

What makes the standing stones present there so intriguing

What makes the Coëby cemetery unique

What could the discovery reveal about Neolithic people

Archaeologists investigating a Neolithic cemetery in Brittany, France, may have uncovered clues to a burial tradition that dates back around 7,000 years. At the Coëby Neolithic cemetery near Trédion, researchers examined two unusually large, elongated earth mounds whose purpose has remained uncertain since the site was discovered in 1986.In a recent study published in ‘ Archaeological Prospection ,’ Philippe Gouézin and Vivien Mathé used electrical surveys to look beneath the surface of the two structures without excavating them. Their findings suggest that the mounds could contain stone-built burial chambers and unusual standing stones, including stones that may have been shaped to resemble people. The researchers say the structures could be related to a type of Neolithic funerary monument known as a Passy-type barrow, potentially extending the known distribution of this tradition further west.Instead of immediately digging into the ancient structures, the researchers used electrical surveys to investigate what could be hidden beneath the surface. The technique allowed them to examine differences in the material inside the mounds. In simple terms, electrical measurements can reveal areas where the ground behaves differently, helping archaeologists identify buried structures without having to disturb them.For the Coëby study, electrical surveys were carried out on two of the long barrows. The researchers were looking for evidence that could explain the internal construction of the mounds and help determine whether they were actually funerary monuments. The results produced patterns that were consistent with structures beneath the earth. According to the study, these findings could indicate arrangements similar to Passy-type monuments, including rough and anthropomorphic standing stones.The evidence points towards that possibility, although the researchers have been careful not to present it as a confirmed conclusion. The survey results suggest that the two long barrows may contain internal stone structures. Other interpretations include the possibility of stone clusters within the mounds. Taken together, these features make a funerary purpose increasingly plausible.This is important because the shape of the Coëby mounds does not immediately fit the more familiar image of a prehistoric burial monument. Rather than being simple piles of earth or stone, the structures appear to have been deliberately built and may have contained carefully arranged elements. The study therefore raises the possibility that the Coëby long barrows were part of a particular Neolithic burial tradition. The researchers say they could be comparable to Passy-type constructions, which are known from areas of northern France.Passy-type monuments are a distinctive form of Neolithic burial structure associated with northern France. Their importance to the Coëby discovery comes from the similarities suggested by the electrical survey. The researchers note that Passy-type constructions are associated with elongated monuments covering unusual stone arrangements, including rough stones and stones with human-like forms.If the Coëby structures are confirmed as examples of this tradition, they could represent a significant geographical extension of where such monuments are known to have existed. That possibility gives the discovery a wider importance. It would not simply add two more prehistoric mounds to the cemetery. It could also show that ideas about how the dead were commemorated travelled across a broader part of Neolithic France than previously recognised.One of the most puzzling elements is the presence of ‘standing stones’ within or around the long barrows. The research points to the possibility that some of these stones were anthropomorphic, meaning that they may have had forms resembling human figures. This is particularly interesting in a burial setting, where such stones could have carried a symbolic meaning connected with the people buried at the site.However, the researchers do not claim to know what these stones represented or how they were used. Their presence remains one of the central mysteries surrounding the monuments. Earlier archaeological work at Coëby has already revealed anthropomorphic stone features elsewhere in the cemetery. Research on other parts of the site has documented complex funerary structures and human-shaped stone elements, showing that the use of unusual standing stones was not entirely isolated within the wider landscape.The Coëby cemetery is located in the commune of Trédion in Morbihan, Brittany. According to the research by Gouézin and Mathé, the site was discovered in 1986 and has since been the focus of archaeological work examining its many megalithic structures. The cemetery is unusual because several different types of prehistoric monuments are concentrated within the same landscape. The researchers described an arrangement that reflects activity from the Neolithic period through to the Bronze Age.The findings offer a glimpse into how communities thousands of years ago may have treated their dead and shaped their landscapes. The Coëby cemetery was not simply a place where bodies were buried. The range of monuments found there suggests that people repeatedly modified and used the landscape over long periods. The newly studied barrows add another layer to that history.For Gouézin and Mathé, the electrical survey provides a way to investigate these structures while leaving them largely undisturbed. It has also produced evidence that can guide future archaeological work. The researchers stress that further investigation is needed. Excavation would be necessary to establish exactly what lies inside the mounds and to determine whether the suspected structures are genuinely funerary.
Article Summary: Archaeologists have uncovered clues to a burial tradition that dates back around 7,000 years. At the Coëby Neolithic cemetery near Trédion, researchers examined two unusually large, elongated earth mounds whose purpose has remained uncertain since the site was discovered in 1986. Instead of immediately digging into the ancient structures, the researchers used electrical surveys to investigate what could be hidden beneath the surface. Their findings suggest that the mounds could contain stone-built burial chambers and unusual standing stones.

Article Title: Meet Zac Waters, the 13-year-old Utah boy who spent 300 hours 3D-printing a wheelchair for a 21-month-old girl
Article Text:
Zac's summer project was a custom wheelchair designed for a 21-month-old girl. (News 4 Utah- screengrab) - Enhanced using AI for clarity.

A summer well spent

Family's support

Wanting to build more

While many children his age were on summer break, 13-year-old Zac Waters spent about 300 hours working on a very different project. The Lehi, Utah, boy used his 3D printing skills to build a custom mobility chair for a 21-month-old girl.According to ABC 4, Waters became interested in 3D printing after watching YouTube videos about the technology. He soon wanted to use what he was learning for something beyond simply making objects. That search led him to MakeGood, a New Orleans-based nonprofit that provides free 3D-printed mobility devices for children with disabilities.The organisation's volunteer network allows people with 3D printers to make mobility devices at home. Its open-source Toddler Mobility Trainer design can be built for about $150 in materials.Waters found an opportunity to combine his interest in 3D printing with his wish to help someone in need. He was matched through MakeGood's volunteer network with a 21-month-old girl and began working on a mobility chair made specifically for her.The project took up much of Waters' summer. He spent roughly 300 hours designing, printing, testing and assembling the chair before it was ready.The finished mobility chair was customised for the toddler. It has pink accents because pink is her favourite colour. Waters also added a removable cupholder and tray table to make the chair more useful for her.The chair was also designed with her needs as she grows. Its footrest and headrest can be adjusted, while the back panel has space for heavier medical equipment. The straps were printed using a soft, flexible material for comfort.For Waters, the project brought together two things he enjoys most. “It combines my two favorite things in life: 3D printing and helping people in need. It just makes sense!” Waters told ABC4.He said one of his favourite parts of 3D printing is putting individual pieces together. The wheelchair gave him a chance to work on that process over and over again as he designed and tested the different parts.Although Waters did much of the work himself, his family supported him throughout the project. His grandmother, Charlotte Waters, said the family helped keep him on track while allowing him to work through his own ideas.Zac compared the support to bowling ball training rails, saying his family helped him bounce ideas around as he worked towards completing the chair.For Charlotte, the project was about more than what her grandson could make with a 3D printer. She hopes the experience will remain with him as he grows older.“We hope he always remembers that the greatest legacy anyone can leave is to make someone else’s life better,” she said.The family said the project showed that being young does not prevent someone from helping another person.The experience has also shaped what Waters wants to do next. He plans to continue developing his 3D printing skills and hopes to reach the level of expertise of the MakeGood engineering team.He has not decided on a specific career yet, but when asked what he wants to do when he grows up, he saiys he wants to do “something techie.”Waters' project is part of a wider volunteer effort run by MakeGood. The nonprofit was founded in 2021 by certified healthcare architect Noam Platt.MakeGood has delivered more than 1,000 Toddler Mobility Trainers through its volunteer network. Despite this, more than 550 requests for the devices are still pending.The average wait for a chair is about 70 days. MakeGood's fundraising page also says that more than 2 million children in the US need a mobility device they do not have.
Article Summary: Zac Waters, 13, used his 3D printing skills to build a custom wheelchair for a 21-month-old girl. The Lehi, Utah, boy spent about 300 hours designing, printing, testing and assembling the chair before it was ready. The project is part of a wider volunteer effort run by MakeGood.

Article Title: Archaeologists uncover human-shaped stones linked to a mysterious Bronze Age burial site in Britain
Article Text:
Image: La Rochelle University

How a strange discovery is changing what researchers know about Coëby cemetery

The human-shaped stones are what make the site particularly unusual

What the cemetery reveals about Bronze Age ideas of death

Why technology is helping archaeologists revisit ancient landscapes

The mystery of Coëby is far from solved

A Bronze Age burial site in Britain is raising new questions about how prehistoric communities treated their dead after archaeologists identified unusual stone objects shaped in ways that may resemble human bodies. The discovery comes from research into the Coëby cemetery, a prehistoric burial landscape in Lincolnshire that contains a series of burial mounds dating back thousands of years.The unusual stones are among several features that make the site difficult to interpret. Rather than being ordinary pieces of naturally occurring rock, some appear to have been deliberately selected or modified and placed in contexts associated with prehistoric burials.A study titled ‘ Atypical Long Barrows in the Cöeby Neolithic Cemetery (Trédion, Morbihan, France)? The Contribution of Electrical Surveys ’ examined the site using archaeological and geophysical evidence, adding another layer to the mystery surrounding Coëby and the practices of the people who used the cemetery.Coëby is part of a wider prehistoric landscape in Lincolnshire containing monuments and burial sites created during the Bronze Age. Burial mounds were an important feature of prehistoric Britain, but the people who constructed them did not always treat the dead in the same way.Some individuals were buried with objects, while others were cremated and their remains placed in vessels or pits. Across Britain, archaeologists have also found evidence that burial monuments were repeatedly modified, reused and incorporated into later landscapes.The Coëby cemetery provides an opportunity to examine these changing practices because its remains preserve evidence of several prehistoric activities within the same landscape.The recent study, published in Archaeological Prospection, used archaeological investigation to reassess features associated with the cemetery and explore what they might reveal about how the site was constructed and used. The research adds new evidence to the continuing investigation of Coëby's prehistoric remains.Among the most intriguing discoveries are stones whose shapes appear to evoke human forms. Such objects are potentially important because deliberately shaped stones can provide clues about how prehistoric communities represented people, the dead or the human body.However, their interpretation requires caution. A stone that resembles a human figure does not necessarily represent an intentional sculpture. Natural weathering, erosion and the shape of the original stone can sometimes produce surprisingly recognisable forms.This is why archaeologists examine not only an object's appearance but also its archaeological context. Where was it found? Was it deliberately placed? Does it show evidence of modification? Was it associated with a burial or monument? And are similar objects found elsewhere?These questions are particularly important at Coëby because the stones cannot be understood separately from the wider burial landscape.Bronze Age burial monuments were not simply places where bodies were deposited and forgotten. Across prehistoric Britain, burial sites appear to have been spaces where communities returned repeatedly, altered monuments and interacted with the remains of earlier generations.The presence of unusual stones at Coëby may therefore point towards a more complicated relationship with the dead. If the stones were deliberately shaped or selected to resemble human figures, they could potentially have played a symbolic role in ceremonies or commemorative practices.But archaeologists have not established a single explanation for their purpose. The evidence allows several possibilities, and further research will be needed to determine whether the human-like appearance was intentional.Modern archaeological investigations increasingly combine traditional excavation with non-invasive techniques that allow researchers to investigate buried remains without disturbing them.At prehistoric burial sites, this can be especially valuable. Geophysical surveys can reveal buried ditches, pits, mound boundaries and other features that are difficult to see from the surface. Researchers can then compare those results with excavation records and previously recovered objects.The research published in Archaeological Prospection demonstrates how reassessing older archaeological landscapes with modern methods can produce new questions even when the monuments themselves have been known for decades.Rather than treating a prehistoric cemetery as a collection of isolated graves, archaeologists can now examine how its different features relate to one another and reconstruct how people may have moved through and interacted with the landscape.The human-shaped stones are intriguing precisely because they raise more questions than they answer. If prehistoric people intentionally selected or shaped them to resemble human forms, their presence could provide rare evidence for how Bronze Age communities represented the human body outside conventional figurative art.If their shapes are instead the result of natural processes, they still demonstrate how easily modern observers can project familiar forms onto ancient objects.For now, Coëby remains a landscape where the physical evidence offers tantalising clues but few definitive answers. The burial mounds, unusual stones and other archaeological features together suggest that the site had a complex history of use.The new research does not close the mystery. Instead, it makes the cemetery even more interesting by showing how much may still be hidden beneath and around Britain's prehistoric burial monuments.
Article Summary: Discovery comes from research into the Coëby cemetery in Lincolnshire. It contains a series of burial mounds dating back thousands of years. The unusual stones are among several features that make the site difficult to interpret. Some appear to have been deliberately selected or modified and placed in contexts associated with prehistoric burials.

Article Title: A Texas homeowner thought they had a snake problem. Then more than 20 rattlesnakes emerged from beneath the house
Article Text:
More than 20 rattlesnakes found beneath a Texas home

Texas is home to several rattlesnake species

Homeowners should not attempt to remove rattlesnakes

How to make a home less attractive to snakes

A routine wildlife-removal call in Aledo, Texas, turned into a startling discovery when specialists found more than 20 rattlesnakes living beneath a home. The homeowners had initially sought help with what appeared to be a typical animal-removal problem, but snake wrangler Sheila Taber soon realised the situation was far more serious. As the team worked in the crawl space, snakes continued to emerge, prompting Taber to describe the site as “a whole den”. Dallas Fort Worth Wildlife Control eventually removed more than 20 rattlesnakes from beneath the residence, with company owner Randall Kennedy estimating the final count at roughly two dozen. The discovery highlighted how easily wildlife can find shelter in spaces around human homes.According to NBC 5 DFW, the wildlife-control team discovered a large group of rattlesnakes in the crawl space beneath the Aledo property. Taber, who has more than a decade of experience handling snakes, said the job initially appeared relatively straightforward. However, the number of snakes continued to increase as the team searched the area. “That was a whole den. They just kept coming out,” she said. Dallas Fort Worth Wildlife Control ultimately removed more than 20 rattlesnakes, while Kennedy said the final number was approximately two dozen.The space beneath the house appears to have offered several conditions that made it attractive to snakes. According to the report, the crawl space was cooler than the hot conditions outside and contained a ready supply of prey. Kennedy said rats and rabbits were present beneath the home, providing an available food source for the rattlesnakes. Texas Parks and Wildlife Department notes that snakes may be attracted to residential areas because they provide food and shelter. Rodents around homes can therefore indirectly attract predators that feed on them.Rattlesnakes are a natural part of the Texas ecosystem and are found across large parts of the state. Texas Parks and Wildlife Department says Texas has 10 species of rattlesnakes, while the western diamondback is the state's most widespread rattlesnake. It can be found across much of Texas, although it is absent from the easternmost part of the state. Rattlesnakes play an ecological role as predators, helping regulate populations of rodents and other small animals.The discovery does not necessarily mean the snakes deliberately targeted the home. Wildlife often makes use of spaces that provide protection from predators, extreme weather and other threats. A crawl space can offer shade and relatively stable temperatures, while rodents living nearby can provide food. In this case, the combination appears to have created conditions suitable for a sizeable concentration of snakes. Kennedy described the situation by noting that if a space feels comfortable to people, it can also provide attractive conditions for snakes.Although rattlesnakes generally avoid people, coming across one unexpectedly can be dangerous because they are venomous and may strike when they feel threatened. Texas Parks and Wildlife Department advises people who encounter rattlesnakes to stop, locate the snake and slowly move away rather than approaching it. The danger becomes more significant when snakes are hidden beneath a house, because residents may unknowingly enter a confined space where they are difficult to see. Children and pets can also be at greater risk if they come too close to a snake.Wildlife experts advise against trying to capture or kill venomous snakes. The safest option is to keep a safe distance and contact trained wildlife-removal professionals or local animal-control authorities. The CDC similarly recommends contacting animal control or wildlife professionals when a wild animal poses a potential danger around a home. People should also keep children and pets away from the area until the animal has been safely dealt with.Homeowners can take several steps to reduce the chances of snakes settling around their properties. Texas Parks and Wildlife Department recommends controlling rodents, removing potential hiding places and sealing openings that could allow snakes to enter buildings. Gaps around doors, windows, pipes, foundations and other parts of a structure should be inspected and sealed where appropriate. Removing piles of debris, wood and other materials can also reduce potential shelter for rodents and snakes.Anyone who encounters a rattlesnake should avoid approaching it or attempting to move it. The safest response is to back away slowly and give the snake plenty of space. If it is inside or immediately around a home, a qualified wildlife professional should be contacted for removal.
Article Summary: More than 20 rattlesnakes were found living in a crawl space beneath a home in Aledo, Texas. Wildlife experts removed more than 20 of the snakes from beneath the home. The discovery highlighted how easily wildlife can find shelter in spaces around human homes.

Article Title: In 1969, US engineers buried an experimental nuclear reactor under a grassy mound in Nebraska; the reactor still lies underground today
Article Text:
​Representative Image of a grassy mound concealing a decommissioned nuclear reactor beside an active coal power plant (AI-generated image)

Why the Hallam reactor was built in the first place

How technical problems ended the reactor's short working life

What decommissioning crews actually did to seal the site

Why officials chose to bury rather than fully remove the reactor

How long the site will remain under federal watch

What the Hallam site says about America's early nuclear experiments

In the late 1950s, the United States Atomic Energy Commission built an experimental nuclear power plant near the small town of Hallam, Nebraska, hoping to prove that a sodium-cooled, graphite-moderated reactor could reliably generate electricity for the commercial grid. It never quite worked as planned. Persistent technical failures forced operators to shut the reactor down after less than two years of active operation, and by 1969, decommissioning crews had dismantled the aboveground facility entirely, sealed the reactor's most contaminated components in place, and covered the entire underground structure with six feet of earth. What remains today is a 1.4-acre, flat-topped mound of grass sitting on the edge of an active coal power plant, quietly containing a reactor vessel that federal regulators expect to keep monitoring for more than a century after the plant went dark.The site has since become an unusual reminder of the early experimental era of nuclear energy, when engineers were testing reactor concepts with limited operational experience. Although the facility produced electricity for only a short period, its buried remains continue to demonstrate how the consequences of experimental nuclear projects can persist long after operations end.The Hallam Nuclear Power Facility formed part of the Atomic Energy Commission's wider Power Demonstration Reactor Program, an effort launched in the 1950s to test whether various experimental reactor designs could realistically compete with conventional coal-fired power plants. According to an official fact sheet published by the United States Department of Energy , the original facility used a 240-megawatt thermal reactor cooled by liquid sodium and moderated by graphite, a design the Atomic Energy Commission operated from 1962 to 1964 as part of that broader demonstration effort.The plant sat on the grounds of what is now the Sheldon Power Station, an active coal-fired facility roughly 19 miles south of Lincoln, still owned and operated by the Nebraska Public Power District today.The Hallam reactor's operational record turned out to be brief and troubled almost from the start. After reaching criticality in 1962, the plant was shut down within just two years because of persistent problems with its graphite moderator, according to a technical report on the facility filed with the Department of Energy's Office of Scientific and Technical Information. Although the Atomic Energy Commission formally declared the reactor's research objectives fulfilled by 1966, the technology itself never demonstrated the kind of reliable, sustained performance needed to justify continued operation, and the commission ultimately moved toward shutting the project down rather than attempting further repairs.Decommissioning and dismantling work ran from 1967 through 1969, and the process involved carefully separating what could be removed from what needed to stay permanently sealed underground. Crews demolished nearly all of the facility's aboveground structures, removed all bulk sodium coolant from the site, and extracted the reactor core along with most other radioactive materials for disposal elsewhere. What could not be safely removed remained entombed within the underground reactor building itself, spread across three separate contamination zones, one holding the reactor vessel and its surrounding containment structures, a second containing fuel storage thimbles, and a third housing damaged moderator elements sealed inside storage cells. Engineers used steam to deactivate any residual sodium left in the structure, guarding against the risk of hydrogen gas forming if groundwater ever breached the sealed chamber.Rather than attempting a complete removal of every contaminated component, a costly and technically demanding undertaking even by today's standards, engineers opted to entomb the reactor's remaining radioactive material in place and cover the entire underground structure with soil. The result was the distinctive 1.4-acre, flat-topped mound that still defines the site today, engineered with sloped sides specifically to promote water runoff and reduce the risk of erosion exposing the sealed structure beneath. Documents describing the exact layout, dimensions and precise location of the buried reactor vessel remain sealed inside stainless steel boxes secured at two separate points on the property, preserved specifically so future generations retain accurate records of what lies underground long after anyone involved in the original construction is gone.Responsibility for the site now falls to the Department of Energy's Office of Legacy Management, which conducts regular surveillance and environmental monitoring to confirm the entombed materials remain safely contained. That oversight includes periodic groundwater sampling around the mound to check for any sign of radiological contamination migrating away from the sealed structure, alongside routine visual inspections of the grass cover and surrounding erosion controls. Based on radioactive decay calculations, the Department of Energy estimates the site could potentially be released for unrestricted use around the year 2070, roughly a century after decommissioning was completed, though continued monitoring commitments extend even further, with some agreements calling for oversight to continue until 2090.Hallam was never an isolated case. Similar sodium-cooled test reactors built under the same federal demonstration program, including one in Piqua, Ohio, met comparable fates, shut down after a handful of operating years and entombed on-site rather than fully dismantled. Together, these early experimental plants represent a formative and often overlooked chapter in America's nuclear power history, a period when engineers tested a wide range of reactor designs to see which technologies might scale into commercial use and which would not. Hallam's grassy mound stands today as a quiet, largely unnoticed monument to that uncertain era, a reminder that some of the twentieth century's boldest energy experiments left behind consequences still being carefully managed generations later, hidden in plain sight beneath an ordinary-looking field.
Article Summary: The Hallam Nuclear Power Facility was built in the 1950s as part of the Atomic Energy Commission's Power Demonstration Reactor Program. The plant was shut down after less than two years of operation due to technical problems with the reactor's graphite moderator. The site is now a 1.4-acre, flat-topped mound of grass sitting on the edge of an active coal power plant.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.
